analysis.body:
No Census adoption figure appears in the source set for defense, so measured adoption is not directly reported. What is available is the federal procurement record. SAM.gov is the primary record of federal contract opportunities, including AI-related DoD solicitations, awards, and vendor registrations, free and searchable. USAspending.gov carries every federal award as downloadable data, built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed, so contract spending on AI-related solutions traces there. FPDS records DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level. No dollar amounts or vendor concentration figures are reported in these excerpts.

The Defense Innovation Unit is the commercial on-ramp. Its stated mission is to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power, and it is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on the procurement record: its platform layer transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Govini tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy, and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending. Silicon Valley Defense Group monitors the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security, publicly mapping the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space. Specific use cases are not enumerated in these excerpts beyond AI and autonomy as tracked categories.

Janes and Forecast International cover the defense-industrial base as long-running analysis providers, maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts; they are subscription sources. Janes describes its work as validated open source defense and security intelligence, covering military platforms, threat intelligence, and industry awareness, with data governance and peer review to produce decision-grade intelligence.

The World of AI's Government Labs section is described as tracking federal AI research organisations, but the two entries currently listed are Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China. Both are state-funded and draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, and both can command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

The sources do not report ROI evidence for defense AI deployments. On the regulatory and security side, SAM.gov states that the federal procurement system is for official use only, subject to monitoring, and contains Controlled Unclassified Information protected under 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2. Unauthorized activities are subject to disciplinary action including criminal prosecution. This is system security for procurement data, not AI-specific deployment guidance. No AI-specific regulatory posture is described in the source set.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical starting point is the free federal procurement data: SAM.gov for solicitations, USAspending.gov for awards, and FPDS for transaction-level contract actions. Govini's scorecards and Silicon Valley Defense Group's mapping add vendor and capital context, while Janes and Forecast International provide subscription forecasts of the defense-industrial base. The Defense Innovation Unit is the designated commercial gateway. The source set does not provide adoption rates, ROI figures, or AI-specific regulatory rules, so those questions remain open on this record.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues two individually verified government AI labs: Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China. It says each classification is based on a document the organisation published about itself, with the source and date recorded, rather than assigned by keyword or model. The text notes that state-funded government labs carry public mandates and draw on sovereign budgets, which shapes what they build. It contrasts TII, which operates under Abu Dhabi’s Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models, with Shanghai AI Laboratory, backed by national ministries and municipal government. Both institutions can, in principle, command infrastructure commitments that market-driven labs must negotiate commercially.
